row.name: Horvat Shema
row.description: Khirbet Shema is an archaeological site located in Israel at the foot of Mount Meron [1]. It features the ruins of a large Jewish village of the Roman and Byzantine periods, including the remains of an ancient synagogue and a mausoleum [1]. American archaeologist Eric M. Meyers excavated the site from 1970 to 1972 on behalf of the American Schools of Oriental Research [1]. The area recovered exceeded six acres [1]. Excavations have uncovered a large mausoleum, numerous tombs and an ancient synagogue [1].

row.name: Roundton Hill
row.description: Roundton Hill is a steep-sided volcanic hill rising to 370 metres in eastern Montgomeryshire, Powys, Wales, near the English border at Church Stoke [1] [2]. Now managed as a nature reserve by the Montgomeryshire Wildlife Trust since 1985, old lead and barites mines on the hill provide roosting habitat for bats [1] [3].

row.name: Gonnus
row.description: Gonnus or Gonnos or Gonni was a town and polis of the Perrhaebi in ancient Thessaly, which derived its name, according to the later Greek critics, from Gonneus [1]. Its position made it one of the most important places in the north of Thessaly [1]. It stood on the northern side of the Peneius, near the entrance of the only two passes by which an enemy can penetrate into Thessaly from the north [1]. The celebrated vale of Tempe begins to narrow at Gonnus; and the pass across Mount Olympus a little to the west of Tempe leads into Thessaly at Gonnus [1]. It was by the latter route that the army of Xerxes I entered Thessaly [1]. After the Battle of Cynoscephalae (197 BCE), Philip V of Macedon fled in haste to Tempe, but halted a day at Gonnus, to receive such of his troops as might have survived the battle [1]. Gonnus does not occur in history after the wars of the Romans in Greece, but it is mentioned by Strabo and Ptolemy [1]. The editors of the Barrington Atlas of the Greek and Roman World locate Gonnus at the modern town of Gonnoi [1].

row.name: El Tintal
row.description: El Tintal is a Maya archaeological site in the northern Petén region of Guatemala, located about 25 km northeast of Carmelita [1]. It is the second-largest site in the Mirador Basin, after El Mirador itself, and ranks among the four largest sites in northern Petén [1]. El Tintal was linked to El Mirador by a causeway [1].

row.name: Castulo
row.description: Castulo was an ancient Iberian settlement in the province of Jaén, Andalusia, Spain, near modern Linares, occupied from the Neolithic period [1] [2]. By the 6th century BC, it served as the chief settlement of the Oretani people [1] [2]. According to Roman sources, the princess Himilce married Carthaginian general Hannibal [1] [3]. Castulo later became a Christian bishopric, now a Latin titular see [1].

row.name: Tiverton, Devon
row.description: Tiverton is a town at the confluence of the rivers Exe and Lowman in Devon, England, with human occupation dating to the Stone Age, evidenced by numerous flint tools found in the area [1]. Cranmore Castle is one of the largest enclosures in Devon at over 15 acres, with clear sightlines to other earthworks and overlooking the river confluence [2]. Its function remains debated -- possibly a livestock enclosure, market site, or tribal oppidum [2]. The town's name derives from "Twy-ford-ton," meaning "the town on two fords" [3].

row.name: Pumawasi, Anta
row.description: Pumawasi is a large pre-Columbian rock art cave in the Chinchaypujio District of Cusco, measuring 22 m deep, 30 m wide, and 19 m high [1] [2]. Ceramics and human bone remains indicate use as both a burial ground and ceremonial site [1] [2].

row.name: Cumae
row.description: Cumae was the first ancient Greek colony on mainland Italy, founded around 725 BC by Euboean settlers from Chalcis [1] [2]. It became a major power in Campania, spreading Greek culture and the Euboean alphabet variant that eventually became the Latin alphabet [1]. The site is famed as home of the Cumaean Sibyl, Apollo's oracle, whose purported 130-metre underground corridor was identified by archaeologist Amedeo Maiuri in 1932 [1] [2].

row.name: Franchthi Cave
row.description: Franchthi Cave is a major archaeological site overlooking Kiladha Bay in the Argolic Gulf, southeastern Greece [1]. The site documents the full transition from Paleolithic hunter-gatherers to Neolithic farmers, with domesticated plants and animals appearing around 7,000 BC [1] [2]. Finds include stone tools, pottery, and Mesolithic child burials now displayed in the Nafplion Archaeological Museum [3].

row.name: Apazzu

row.name: Jisk'a Iru Muqu
row.description: Jisk'a Iru Muqu is a pre-Columbian open-air site in the Aymara community of Jachacachi, 54 km southeast of Puno, Peru, in the Lake Titicaca Basin [1]. Occupied from c. 3400-1600 BCE (Late Archaic to Early Formative), it was the first Archaic open-air site excavated in the Titicaca Basin, discovered by Mark Aldenderfer in 1994 [1] [2] [3]. Excavations recovered obsidian tools, a gold necklace, and early domestic architecture showing reduced residential mobility [1] [4]. The site provides critical evidence for the transition from mobile foraging to settled village life in the south-central Andes [1] [5].

row.name: Dubris
row.description: Dubris, also known as Portus Dubris and Dubrae, was a port in Roman Britain on the site of present-day Dover, Kent, England [1]. At the start of his first attempt to conquer Britain in 55 BC Julius Caesar initially tried to land at Dubris, whose natural harbour had presumably been identified by Volusenus as a suitable landing place [1]. Two lighthouses, each called the "Pharos", were built at Dover soon after the Roman conquest [1]. At its peak, Dubris was a major trading centre, taking over from Rutupiae as the main Roman cross-Channel port [1]. With Rutupiae, it was one of the starting points for Watling Street, the Roman road to Canterbury and, ultimately, London [1]. During the construction of the new A256/York Street bypass in the 1970s, Roman remains were discovered and an eight-week excavation followed [1]. The archaeologists discovered a Roman mansio now known as the "Roman Painted House" [1]. Dubris's mansio was demolished in 270 for the construction of a Saxon Shore fort [1].

row.name: Dinedor Camp
row.description: Dinedor Camp is an Iron Age hillfort, about 1 kilometre west of the village of Dinedor and about 3 kilometres south of Hereford in England [1]. The fort is on a spur of Dinedor Hill; it overlooks to the east the River Wye at the confluence with the River Lugg [1]. It is about 337 metres long and 160 metres wide, enclosing an area of about 3.8 hectares [1]. There is an out-turned entrance at the east [1]. There is a steep natural slope on the south side, and a single rampart, about 3 metres high, around the rest of the fort, rising to about 8 metres in the north-east [1]. There was some excavation in 1951 at the north-east of the fort, a trench being cut from the edge of the rampart for about 35 metres towards the centre of the camp [1]. Sherds of Iron Age and Roman pottery, part of an iron axehead and other iron fragments were found [1].

row.name: Ərəbyengicə
row.description: An ancient settlement in the Sharur District of the Nakhchivan Autonomous Republic, Azerbaijan, situated about 200 meters north of the Araz River [1]. Dating to the 4th-3rd millennia BC, the site covers approximately 0.8 hectares and preserves cultural layers from both the Eneolithic period and the Kura-Araxes culture [1]. Archaeological finds include obsidian remains, chaff-faced and chaff-tempered pottery, and combed-surface ceramics typical of the Late Chalcolithic of the Nakhchivan region [1]. The monument has been significantly damaged by agricultural activity [1].

row.name: Ninamarca
row.description: Ninamarca (possibly from Quechua nina fire, marka village, "fire village") is an archaeological site in Peru [1]. It is located in the Cusco Region, Paucartambo Province, Colquepata District, southeast of Colquepata near the village of Ninamaca [1]. There are about 30 chullpas of pre-Inca times situated on top of a mountain at about 3,000 m [1].

row.name: Chedworth Roman Villa
row.description: Chedworth Roman Villa is located near Chedworth, Gloucestershire, England and is a scheduled monument [1]. It is one of the largest and most elaborate Roman villas so far discovered in Britain and one with the latest occupation beyond the Roman period [1]. The villa was built in phases from the early 2nd century to the 5th century, with the 4th-century construction transforming the building into an elite dwelling arranged around three sides of a courtyard [1]. The 4th-century building included a heated and furnished west wing containing a dining-room with a fine mosaic floor, as well as two separate bathing suites: one for damp-heat and one for dry-heat [1]. The villa was accidentally discovered in 1864 by Thomas Margetts, a gamekeeper who was digging for a ferret [1]. The site was subsequently excavated in 1865-7 by James Farrer [1].

row.name: Hartashen Megalithic Avenue
row.description: The site consists of two avenues of megalithic rocks which do not intersect [1] [2]. These avenues are composed of basalt stones which are placed at an angle, and menhirs are arranged in three rows in each [1] [2]. The purpose of these three rows of menhirs in unclear and further research is underway [1] [2]. There is no firm dating of the site [1] [3].

row.description: Qaqapatan is an archaeological site with rock paintings located in the Pasco Region of Peru, within Yarusyacan District [1]. row.name: Deriivka
row.description: Deriivka is a Copper Age settlement and cemetery on the right bank of the Dnieper in Kirovohrad Oblast, Ukraine, dating to c. 4500-3500 BC and associated with the Sredny Stog culture [1] [2]. The site gained fame for a high percentage of horse bones and a horse burial with apparent bit wear, initially interpreted as the earliest evidence of horse domestication and riding [1] [3] [4]. However, radiocarbon dating later showed the horse skull dated to the Iron Age (c. 700-200 BC), undermining claims of 4th-millennium horseback riding [1] [5] [6].

row.name: Arch of Janus
row.description: The only surviving quadrifrons (four-faced) arch in Rome, standing 16 m high on a 12 m square base in the Forum Boarium [1] [2] [3]. Built using spolia from earlier buildings, it may honor Constantine I or Constantius II [1]. Each of its four passageways measures 10.6 m high, and the piers contain 48 niches across two tiers [1] [3] [4]. The Frangipane family converted it into a fortress tower in the Middle Ages [1] [5].

row.name: Ivinghoe
row.description: Ivinghoe is a historic market town and a civil parish in the east of Buckinghamshire, in England, near the Hertfordshire and Bedfordshire borders [1]. The name of the place is of Anglo-Saxon origin and is glossed as 'Ifa's hill-spur' [1]. The Domesday Book of 1086 records the settlement under the name Evinghehou [1]. The village stands inside the Chiltern Hills, at the edge of the Chilterns' Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty [1]. Ivinghoe is an important point on the Icknield Way, a route claimed to be the oldest road in Britain, though that claim has been disputed [1]. The parish church of St Mary the Virgin dates from 1220, was burnt in 1234 in an act of spite against the local bishop, and was rebuilt in 1241 [1].

row.name: Abritus
row.description: Abritus was a major Roman fortified city in the province of Moesia Inferior, founded as a military camp near modern Razgrad, Bulgaria [1] [2]. Excavations revealed the largest Late Antique gold treasure found in Bulgaria: 835 coins weighing 4 kg [1] [3]. The archaeological reserve, established in 1984, spans 250 acres [3] [4].

row.name: Brewer's Castle
row.description: Brewer's Castle is an Iron Age defended settlement in the Exmoor region of Somerset, situated on a steep, flat-topped knoll at the eastern end of Hawkridge Ridge Wood in the lower Barle Valley, about 3 km north-west of Dulverton [1] [2] [3]. The pear-shaped enclosure follows the natural contours of the knoll, bounded by the River Barle on three sides and Dane's Brook to the south-west, enclosing just under 0.4 ha with internal dimensions of roughly 75 m by 62 m [2]. Two entrances are located on the west and north-east sides [2]. The site is traditionally associated with William Brewer, warden of the Royal Forest of Exmoor from 1216 to 1225 [2].

row.name: Chacamarca Historic Sanctuary
row.description: Chacamarca Historic Sanctuary is a 2,500-hectare protected area in Junin Province, Peru, established on 7 August 1974 at approximately 4,105 metres above sea level [1] [2]. It preserves the site of the Battle of Junin (6 August 1824), a pivotal cavalry engagement in Peru's War of Independence where patriot forces under Simon Bolivar routed Spanish royalist troops [2] [3]. The sanctuary also protects archaeological remains of the Pumpush culture [2]. Inca-era segments of the Qhapaq Nan road network and storage structures called colcas have been documented at the site [1] [2] [4]. The area conserves Andean ecosystems including bofedales wetlands supporting species such as the endemic giant frog of Chinchaycocha [5] [6] [7] [8].

row.name: Papcastle
row.description: Papcastle was the site of Derventio, a Roman fort in what is now Cumbria, England [1]. Initially built in timber, it was reconstructed in stone [1]. Excavations from 2010-2015 revealed the settlement was far larger than previously thought, uncovering one of the most complete Roman water mills found in Britain, a substantial mansio, and a bathhouse [1]. Much of the fort's stonework was reused for Cockermouth Castle in the 12th century [1] [2].

row.name: Dolmen del prado de Lácara
row.description: The Dolmen del prado de Lácara is a megalithic passage tomb located northwest of Mérida in Badajoz province, Spain, beside the EX-214 road connecting Aljucén with La Nava de Santiago [1]. Constructed during the late Neolithic, toward the end of the 4th millennium BC or early 3rd millennium BC, it ranks among the most monumental and well-preserved megalithic sites in Extremadura [1]. The monument was declared a site of cultural interest in 1912 and a National Monument in 1931 [1] [2].

row.name: Merrivale, Devon
row.description: Merrivale is a Bronze Age and Neolithic ceremonial complex on western Dartmoor, Devon [1] [2]. The site includes two double stone rows (the longest stretching 263 metres), a stone circle of 11 granite stones approximately 18 metres in diameter, a standing menhir over 3 metres tall, and several burial cairns [1]. Over 50 roundhouses from a Bronze Age farming settlement spread across the hillside north of the stone rows [1].

row.name: Inka Raqay, Ayacucho
row.description: An Inca archaeological site in Peru's Ayacucho Region, Huanta Province, Iguain District, situated on top of the mountain Allqu Willka [1] [2]. The name derives from Quechua, where "Inka" refers to the Inca Empire and "raqay" means a ruin, shed, storehouse, or dormitory for farm laborers [1].

row.name: Cheqollo
row.description: Cheqollo (from Quechua for 'nightingale') is a pre-Hispanic archaeological site in Peru's Cusco Region, located in San Jeronimo District north of the town of San Jeronimo [1] [2]. The site was declared National Cultural Heritage (Patrimonio Cultural) by Resolucion Directorial Nacional No. 514/2003 [1] [3]. It lies within the broader landscape of Cusco-area archaeological sites that reflect the region's deep Inca and pre-Inca heritage [1] [4] [5].

row.name: Anemospilia
row.description: A Minoan temple on the northern slope of Mount Juktas, Crete, about 7 km from Knossos, excavated in 1979 by Yannis Sakellarakis [1] [2]. The building consists of three rectangular rooms with a north-facing corridor [3] [4]. Destroyed by earthquake around 1700 BC, the site yielded controversial evidence of what excavators interpreted as human sacrifice: a young man found on an altar with a bronze blade and signs of exsanguination [1] [3] [5]. This interpretation remains debated among scholars [1] [5].

row.name: Quriwayrachina, Ayacucho
row.description: Quriwayrachina is an Inca period archaeological site in Peru's Ayacucho Region, Lucanas Province, Carmen Salcedo District [1]. The settlement sits near the mountain Inka Pallanka, venerated as an apu by local communities [1] [2]. It features two platforms known as Hatun Quri Wayrachina and Huch'uy Quri Wayrachina [1]. On April 20, 2011, the site was designated a National Cultural Heritage of Peru through Resolución Viceministerial No. 459-2011-VMPCIC-MC [1] [3].

row.name: Necropolises of Pydna
row.description: The Necropolises of Pydna contain Macedonian tombs situated around ancient Pydna along the historic road connecting Methone to Dion [1]. The burial sites range from the Bronze Age to the early Christian period [1]. Smaller tumuli have been lost to erosion, while rescue excavations have revealed significant archaeological material [1]. Evidence indicates a population decline during the second Greek colonization period [1].

row.name: Desfina
row.description: Desfina is a town in southern Phocis, Greece [1]. The area has far older significance: on the hill of Kastrouli, a fortified Mycenaean settlement from the 13th-12th century BC features Cyclopean walls approximately 1.2-1.4 m wide, tentatively identified with Homeric Anemoreia [1] [2] [3]. The Southern Phokis Regional Project now conducts transdisciplinary research combining classics, archaeochemistry, and digital humanities to study the region's cultural landscape [3].

row.name: Areni-1 Cave
row.description: The Areni-1 cave complex is an ancient multicomponent site, and late Chalcolithic/Early Bronze Age ritual site and settlement, located near the Areni village in southern Armenia along the Arpa River [1]. In 2008, Armenian PhD student and archeologist Diana Zardaryan of the country's Institute of Archaeology discovered the earliest known shoe in the world at the site [1]. In January 2011, the earliest known winery in the world was uncovered in the cave [1]. Later, in September 2011, the discovery of a straw skirt dating to 3,900 years BCE was reported [1]. In 2009, the oldest humanoid brain was discovered in the cave [1]. Three individuals who lived in the Chalcolithic era (c. 5700–6250 years BP), found in the Areni-1 ("Bird's Eye") cave, were identified as belonging to haplogroup L1a [1].

row.name: Pyrri
row.description: Pyrri was an ancient Roman settlement in the Roman province of Pannonia, situated along a road connecting Poetovio (modern Ptuj, Slovenia) in the north to Siscia (modern Sisak, Croatia) in the south [1] [2] [3] [4]. Archaeological evidence and scholarly research suggest the settlement's location corresponds to the present-day village of Komin in the Sveti Ivan Zelina area of Zagreb County, Croatia [1] [5].

row.name: Macedonian Tombs, Korinos
row.description: The Macedonian Tombs at Korinos are near the modern Greek village of Korinos, situated at the site of ancient Pydna [1]. Tomb A, an important Macedonian tomb, was discovered in the mid-19th century [1]. In 1991, a second smaller grave, Tomb B, was discovered and excavated nearby [1].

row.name: Kʼaxob
row.description: Kʼaxob is a Maya archaeological site in Belize occupied from about 800 BC to AD 900 [1] [2] [3]. The site began as a village and expanded significantly during the Early to Late Classic Periods [1] [2] [3]. Research reveals specific ceramic types, evidence of agriculture, and increasing social stratification among its inhabitants [1] [2] [4]. The complex includes numerous household mounds, plazas, and ritual spaces [1] [3].

row.name: Hatun Usnu
row.description: Hatun Usnu (also known as Qatun Ushno de Toccto) is an archaeological site in Peru's Ayacucho Region, Huamanga Province, Chiara District [1]. The name means "big usnu" in Quechua, referring to a pyramid-shaped, terraced ceremonial platform used by the Incas for rituals involving liquid offerings [1] [2] [3].

row.name: Seven Barrows
row.description: Seven Barrows is a Bronze Age barrow cemetery located at Upper Lambourn in the civil parish of Lambourn, Berkshire, England [1] [2]. The site is designated as a biological Site of Special Scientific Interest due to its unimproved chalk grassland supporting over 100 herb species and a rich insect fauna [1] [3]. It is managed by the Berkshire, Buckinghamshire and Oxfordshire Wildlife Trust and is a Scheduled Monument preserving this important prehistoric burial site [1] [3].

row.card: Seven Barrows is a Bronze Age barrow cemetery at Upper Lambourn in Berkshire, England. Its unimproved chalk grassland supports over 100 herb species and a rich insect fauna.

row.name: Barbury Castle
row.description: Barbury Castle is an Iron Age hillfort in Wiltshire, England [1] [2]. Located about 5.5 miles south of Swindon on Barbury Hill, it sits along the ancient Ridgeway route—a prehistoric pathway crossing the chalk downs of southern England [1] [3]. The fortification features two deep defensive ditches and ramparts [1]. The site lies within the Wessex Downs Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty and commands views across the Cotswolds to the River Severn under clear conditions [1].

row.name: Housesteads Roman Fort
row.description: Housesteads Roman Fort was an auxiliary fort on Hadrian's Wall, at Housesteads, Northumberland, England [1]. It is dramatically positioned on the end of the 1-mile-long crag of the Whin Sill over which the Wall runs [1]. The name of the fort has been given as Vercovicium, Borcovicus, Borcovicium, and Velurtion [1]. Hadrian's Wall was begun in AD 122 and included no forts but smaller milecastles but before it was finished there was a change of plan to include forts [1]. Turret 36B on the site was therefore demolished to make way for the fort built in stone around AD 124 with its northern wall overlying the original Broad Wall foundation [1]. A major rebuilding in the late 3rd/early 4th century included interval towers on the walls, a huge horreum and new barracks [1]. In the 2nd century AD, the garrison consisted of an unknown double-sized auxiliary infantry cohort and a detachment of legionaries from Legio II Augusta [1]. By 409 AD the Romans had withdrawn [1].

row.name: Teatro Romano
row.description: The Roman Theatre of Aosta (Teatro Romano) is an ancient theatre in the city of Aosta in the Aosta Valley, northern Italy, built during the Julio-Claudian dynasty [1] [2] [3]. Its imposing 22-metre-high facade wall remains towering over the surrounding urban area [1] [4]. The semicircular cavea and stage were enclosed within a rectangular perimeter wall -- an unusual design among Roman cities, positioned near the Porta Praetoria to facilitate crowd movement [4] [5]. Substantial restoration was carried out in the 1930s under archaeologist Pietro Barocelli, and the theatre continues to host performances today [4] [6] [7].

row.name: Veluška Tumba
row.description: Veluška Tumba is an ancient settlement from Neolithic times, near the village of Porodin in the Republic of Macedonia, close to Bitola [1]. The site is an artificially raised mound shaped like a truncated cone, with an elliptical base laid out east to west [2]. The mound measures 250 m in length, 150 m in width and 0.70 to 5 m in height [2]. The excavations found a cultural layer four metres thick, filled with habitation remains spread over four horizons [2].

row.name: Blackbury Camp
row.description: An Iron Age hillfort near Southleigh in Devon [1] [2]. The oval enclosure measures roughly 200 m by 100 m, defended by a rampart about 3 m high and 10 m wide with an outer ditch up to 12 m across [2]. Its single south entrance was protected by timber gates, possibly within a gate-tower [2]. Excavations uncovered a hut, cooking pit, oven, over 1,000 slingstones, Iron Age pottery, iron slag, whetstones, and spindle whorls [2] [3] [4]. Managed by English Heritage, it is interpreted as a defended homestead of a wealthy Iron Age family [2] [3].

row.name: Taula
row.description: A taula is a megalithic structure on the Mediterranean island of Menorca [1] [2]. These monuments feature a vertical pillar supporting a horizontal capstone, reaching heights of up to 5 metres [1]. A U-shaped wall typically encloses the structure [1]. Their exact purpose remains unknown, though they likely served religious functions [1] [3].

row.name: Huaca Esmeralda
row.description: Huaca La Esmeralda is a Chimu culture archaeological site in Trujillo, Peru, located halfway between the city center and Chan Chan [1] [2]. The rectangular pyramid features two platforms measuring approximately 65 by 41 meters, accessible through central ramps [3]. Its walls display distinctive relief decorations depicting fishing nets with fish, seabirds, waves, and geometric diamond patterns [1] [2] [3]. Buried under sand, it was discovered by a local landowner in 1923 [2].

row.name: Odeon of Herodes Atticus
row.description: The Odeon of Herodes Atticus is a stone Greek theatre structure located on the southwest slope of the Acropolis of Athens, Greece [1]. The building was completed in AD 161 and then renovated in 1950 [1]. The audience stands and the orchestra were restored using Pentelic marble in the 1950s [1].

row.name: Mezine
row.description: Mezine (or Mezyn) is an Epigravettian archaeological site in northern Ukraine, located on the Desna River bank near the village of Mezine in Novhorod-Siverskyi Raion, Chernihiv Oblast [1] [2]. The site holds the most Paleolithic artifact finds in Ukraine [1]. It is known for a set of bracelets engraved with marks possibly representing lunar calendar cycles [1]. Also discovered at Mezine is the earliest known example of a meander pattern, found on an object carved from mammoth ivory to resemble a bird [1] [2] [3].

row.name: Ancient City of Terina
row.description: Terina was an ancient city located on the Piano di Tirena hill in Nocera Terinese about 20 km from Lamezia Terme in Calabria [1]. The site of the city was allegedly found in 1922 by the archaeologist Paolo Orsi near the modern village of Sant'Eufemia Vetere [1]. A systematic archaeological investigation was made from 1997 and coins, inscriptions and other artefacts retrieved from the site can be seen in the Museo Archeologico Lametino in Lamezia Terme [1]. The site is surrounded by two rivers, Savuto and Grande and matches the description by Strabo written around 20 AD [1].

row.name: Remesiana
row.description: Remesiana was a Roman city located beneath modern Bela Palanka in southeastern Serbia [1] [2]. Positioned on the Via Militaris between Naissus and Serdica, it became a major early Christian center under Bishop Nicetas [1] [3] [4] [5]. The site was declared an Archaeological Site of Great Importance in 1987 [1] [3].

row.name: Nausharo
row.description: Nausharo is an archaeological site dating back to the Harappan period, located in Balochistan, Pakistan [1]. The excavations were carried out between 1985 and 1996 by a French team of archaeologists, under the direction of Jean-François Jarrige [1]. Excavations at Nausharo, 6 km from Mehrgarh, revealed a dwelling-site contemporaneous and identical to the later periods of Mehrgarh [1]. The discovery of a pottery workshop at Nausharo revealed fired and unfired pottery pieces and unworked clay, as well as 12 flint blades or blade fragments [1]. Also significant was the discovery of copper traces found on the platforms of two blades examined with a scanning electron microscope and X ray analysis [1]. Somewhere between 2600 BC and 2000 BC, Mehrgarh seems to have been largely abandoned in favor of Nausharo, which became fortified and quite large [1].

row.description: The Cave of Maltravieso in Caceres, Extremadura, was discovered in 1951 when a quarry explosion exposed the cavity [1] [2]. It contains 71 hand stencils created by blowing pigment around hands placed on the walls, along with linear designs and animal paintings [1] [3].

row.name: Carn Brea, Redruth
row.description: Carn Brea is a Neolithic tor enclosure in Cornwall, England, located 1.6 km southwest of Redruth [1]. The fortified hilltop settlement was occupied between 3700 and 3400 BC [1]. Archaeological excavations led by Roger Mercer revealed a 0.81-hectare inner enclosure surrounded by a 4.5-hectare outer rampart, both constructed with massive stone walls [1] [2]. The site represents Neolithic defensive architecture in southwestern England [1] [3].

row.name: Padah-Lin Caves
row.description: The Padah-Lin Caves are limestone caves located in Taunggyi District, Shan State, Burma [1]. It is located near a path from Nyaunggyat to Yebock, on a spur of the Nwalabo mountains within the Panlaung Reserved Forest [1]. There are two caves; the smaller of the two is a rock shelter while the larger cave comprises nine chambers connected by narrow passages in a north-south axis, three large sinkholes that let natural light in, and several active speleothem formations [1]. Red ochre paintings of human hands, fish, bulls, bison, deer and other objects are visible at the rock shelter [1]. More than 300 cupules have been documented in the rockshelter [1]. Excavations at the rock shelter from 1969 to 1972 recovered seven pieces of charcoal and bone that were radiocarbon dated to between 1,750 and 13,000 years BP [1]. The excavation also recovered over 1,600 stone artifacts as well as many pieces of bone and red ochre [1].

row.name: Gerrards Cross
row.description: Gerrards Cross is a town in Buckinghamshire, England, on the lower slopes of the Chiltern Hills near the River Misbourne [1]. The area contains Bulstrode Park Camp, an Iron Age fortified encampment [1]. Located 19 miles west-north-west of central London, it lies south of Chalfont St Peter, bordering Fulmer, Hedgerley, Iver Heath and Stoke Poges [1].

row.name: El Baúl
row.description: El Baúl is a Pre-Columbian archaeological site in present-day Escuintla Department, Guatemala [1]. El Baúl, along with the sites of Bilbao and El Castillo, is part of the Cotzumalhuapa Archaeological Zone [1]. It was occupied during the prehistoric Formative stage of the Americas [1]. The El Baúl acropolis is located 4 km north of Santa Lucía Cotzumalguapa, 550 metres above sea level, 50 kilometres from the Pacific Ocean [1]. Its southern acropolis complex was destroyed in 1997 by urban development and the main groups are now covered by sugar cane fields [1]. The site's geologic context is volcanic; it is located just south of an active stratovolcano, Fuego volcano [1]. The site contains monumental architecture in its acropolis as well as a probable sweatbath and obsidian workshops [1].

row.name: Kuélap
row.description: Kuélap or Cuélap is a walled settlement located in the mountains near the towns of María and Tingo, in the southern part of the region of Amazonas, Peru [1]. Kuélap is located on a limestone ridge on top of a mountain at an elevation of 3000 metres, on the left bank of the Utcubamba River [1]. Kuélap is a now-abandoned walled settlement that covers an area of about six hectares, 584 m from north to south and 110 m at its widest [1]. The walls are 10 to 20 m high with masonry of limestone blocks finely worked (some blocks may weigh 3 tons) [1]. All but five of the 421 structures in the site are circular; those five are quadrilateral [1]. Human occupation at the site starts in the 5th century AD, but the majority of structures were built between 900 and 1100 AD [1]. The city may have had some 3000 inhabitants, but was abandoned in 1570 due to the Spanish Conquest [1]. Kuélap was accidentally rediscovered in 1843, by Juan Crisóstomo Nieto, a judge from the city of Chachapoyas [1].

row.name: Alderman's Barrow
row.description: Alderman's Barrow is a Bronze Age bowl barrow on Exmoor, England, serving as a burial chamber and later a boundary marker for the parishes of Exford, Exmoor, Luccombe, and Porlock [1] [2]. The turf-covered mound measures 24 by 22 meters and stands 1.4 meters high [2]. Known as Osmunesburgh in the 13th century and Owlaman's Burrow in the 17th century, it received its current name in 1782 [1] [2]. It was scheduled as a protected monument in 1934 [1].

row.description: Torre dels Escipions is a Roman funerary tower built in the early 1st century AD along the Via Augusta, 6 km from ancient Tarraco (modern Tarragona), capital of Hispania Citerior [1] [2]. The tower likely served as a family mausoleum for a married couple or two brothers, housing cremated remains [3].

row.name: Ballylumford Dolmen
row.description: Portal tomb on the Islandmagee peninsula, County Antrim, Northern Ireland, situated in a private front garden near Ballylumford power station [1] [2]. Known locally as the Druid's Altar, it consists of four upright stones supporting a heavy capstone, with a fallen stone inside that may have blocked the tomb entrance [1] [3]. A wall plaque dates it to approximately 2000-1600 BC, though it could be the remains of an even earlier passage grave [1]. It is a State Care Historic Monument in the townland of Ballylumford [1].

row.name: Asclepieion of Pergamon
row.description: The Asclepieion of Pergamon was an asclepieion, a healing temple, built in honour of the gods Asclepius and Hygieia, located west of the Pergamon hill, roughly three kilometers southwest of the acropolis in modern-day Bergama [1]. Founded in the mid-4th century BCE, it functioned as a religious and therapeutic centre through the Hellenistic and Roman periods, reaching its greatest prominence in the 2nd Century CE [1]. The Asclepieion grew across several distinct building phases spanning roughly eight centuries [1]. The sanctuary's origins date to the mid-4th century BCE, when the complex consisted of a modest sacred enclosure and spring shrine at the site [1]. Under the Attalid dynasty in the 3rd and 2nd centuries BCE, the sanctuary saw its major expansion [1]. During this period, a Doric temple to Hygieia was built, along with a cluster of structures around the incubation area [1].

row.name: Ara trium Galliarum
row.description: The Ara trium Galliarum ("Altar of the Three Gauls") was a Roman sanctuary at Lugdunum (modern Lyon, France), founded by Drusus at the confluence of the Rhone and Saone rivers [1] [2] [3]. Consecrated to Roma and Augustus, it served as the central meeting place where representatives of the three Gallic provinces -- Aquitania, Belgica, and Lugdunensis -- gathered annually [1] [2]. The altar bore the names of 60 Gallic tribes and featured prominently on coins from the Lugdunum mint [2] [3].

row.name: House of Taga
row.description: An archaeological site near San Jose Village on Tinian Island, Northern Mariana Islands, featuring prehistoric latte stone pillars unique to the Mariana Islands [1] [2]. The twelve original megaliths stood approximately 15 feet tall, each consisting of a base (haligi) topped with a hemispherical capstone (tasa) [1] [3]. Dating to the Latte Era, this is the largest known latte site in the Marianas [3] [4]. Named after a legendary chief of superhuman strength, only one pillar remains standing today, the others toppled by earthquakes and WWII bombardment in 1944 [1] [3]. Listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1974 [5].

row.name: Ringsbury Camp
row.description: An Iron Age multivallate hillfort dating to approximately 50 BC in the parish of Purton, Wiltshire [1] [2]. The scheduled monument encloses 3.4 hectares within double banks: the inner bank rises 5 metres high surrounded by a 3-metre ditch, while the outer bank stands 2 metres high [1]. The banks are built from non-local limestone rubble, suggesting transported material [1] [2]. Neolithic flint tools and an Iron Age coin (now in Purton Museum) have also been found at the site [1].

row.name: Dzibilnocac
row.description: Dzibilnocac is a Maya archaeological site in Campeche, Mexico, in the central Chenes region near the community of Vicente Guerrero [1]. Initial occupation dates to around 500 BC during the Middle Preclassic period, with its peak development occurring in the Late Classic period when it became a large city and important regional political center with its own emblem glyph [1] [2]. While the architectural style is predominantly Chenes—characterized by elaborately decorated facades—the main Palace exhibits a distinct Rio Bec design [3] [4].

row.name: Peterborough Petroglyphs
row.description: The Peterborough petroglyphs are the largest collection of ancient First Nations petroglyphs (rock carvings) in Ontario [1] [2]. The carvings were created in the pre-Columbian era and represents aspects of First Nations spirituality, including images of shamans, animals, reptiles, and, possibly, the Great Spirit itself [1] [3].

row.name: Kition
row.description: Kition was an ancient city-kingdom on the southern coast of Cyprus, in present-day Larnaca [1]. Phoenicians from Tyre revived the city in the 9th century BC, making it the capital of a Cypriot-Phoenician kingdom [2] [3] [4]. The Kathari site preserves remains of five ancient temples, while the Bamboula acropolis features ship sheds for triremes and a sanctuary dating to at least the 9th century BC [1]. The city was closely linked to copper trade and maritime commerce [1] [3] [5]. Zeno of Citium, founder of Stoic philosophy, was born here c. 334 BC [6] [7].

row.card: Treva is the historical name of a Roman-era settlement in Germany, first recorded by Claudius Ptolemy in the 2nd century AD. Under Augustus, Roman forces reached the Elbe.

row.name: Habloville
row.description: A commune in the Orne department of Normandy, France, containing two Neolithic monuments [1] [2] [3]. The Dolmen des Bignes is a stone table measuring 3.25 by 2.95 metres, located on the border with Neuvy-au-Houlme and classified as a Monument historique in 1931 [2] [4] [5]. Just to the south lies the Tumulus des Hogues listed as a historical monument [2] [6]. Together these sites attest to Neolithic presence and funerary practices in the region [2] [4] [7].

row.name: Temple of Augustus, Pula
row.description: The Temple of Augustus is a well-preserved Roman temple in the city of Pula, Croatia [1]. Dedicated to the first Roman emperor, Augustus, it was probably built during the emperor's lifetime at some point between 27 BC and his death in AD 14 [1]. It was built on a podium with a tetrastyle prostyle porch of Corinthian columns and measures about 8 by 17.3 m, and 14 m high [1]. The richly decorated frieze is similar to that of a somewhat larger and more recent temple, the Maison Carrée in Nîmes [1]. The temple was part of a triad consisting of three temples [1]. The Temple of Augustus stood at the left side of the central temple, and the similar temple of the goddess Diana stood on the other side of the main temple [1]. Under Byzantine rule, the temple was converted into a church, accounting for its survival to modern times, and was later used as a granary [1]. The temple's dedication originally consisted of bronze letters affixed by nails to the stones of the architrave [1].

row.name: Ugarit
row.description: Ugarit was a major ancient port city at Ras Shamra in northern Syria [1] [2] [3]. The site features a grand royal palace with multiple courtyards, plus two acropolis temples dedicated to Baal and Dagan [1] [2]. Excavations yielded texts in multiple languages with parallels to Hebrew biblical poetry [4] [5] [6]. The city was a vital trade hub [3] [5].

row.name: Town Walks, Dorchester
row.description: The Town Walks are tree-lined public promenades in Dorchester, Dorset, following the line of the Roman defences of Durnovaria [1] [2]. The first earthen bank and ditch were constructed no earlier than AD 130, with stone walls added in the 4th century using stone quarried from the Ridgeway near Upwey and cemented with lime mortar [1] [2] [3]. The walks extend across three sides of the rectangular Roman enclosure [2]. Between 1702 and 1743 the ruined walls were landscaped into tree-lined avenues [2] [4]. Only one wall fragment survives, incorporated into a garden wall south of the Top o' Town roundabout [3] [5]. The walks are registered Grade II on the Register of Historic Parks and Gardens [1].

row.name: Ražanj
row.description: Razanj is a municipality in the Nisava District of southern Serbia, situated on the ancient Via Militaris, the Roman military highway [1] [2] [3]. Known as Cametas in Roman times, the settlement served as a stop along this vital route [1] [4]. Archaeological finds recovered during construction work confirm habitation from prehistoric times, with artifacts held in museums in Belgrade and Nis [5].

row.name: Hardknott Roman Fort
row.description: Hardknott Roman Fort is an archeological site, the remains of the Roman fort Mediobogdum, located on the western side of the challenging Hardknott Pass in the English Lake District [1]. The fort was built between 120 and 138 on a rocky spur, and was initially garrisoned by a detachment of the Cohors IV Delmatarum from the Dalmatian coast [1]. It was abandoned around a decade later, then reoccupied circa 200 and remained in use for much of the next two centuries [1]. Leather objects from Roman occupation have been found at the site [1]. The fort is square with rounded corners, 114 metres long externally, or 105 metres internally, the rampart wall being about 1.7 metres thick with ditches adding to the total width of the rampart [1]. The outer wall has four gates, at the centre of each side, and lookout towers at each corner [1]. Within the walls are the remaining outlines of several buildings: two side-by-side granaries, the garrison headquarters building and garrison commander's villa, or Praetorium [1].

row.name: Machu Picchu
row.description: Machu Picchu is a 15th-century Inca citadel located in the Eastern Cordillera of southern Peru on a mountain ridge at 2,430 meters [1]. Studies of skeletal remains found at Machu Picchu show that most people who lived there were immigrants from diverse backgrounds [1]. Excavations documented approximately 104 caves and rock shelters used as burial chambers around Machu Picchu, containing the remains of about 174 individuals, interpreted as largely belonging to yanaconas of diverse ethnic origins rather than the Inca elite [1]. Radiocarbon dating analyses have refined the site's chronology, indicating that Machu Picchu’s main construction and use fall in the early to mid 15th century, slightly earlier than some traditional documentary chronologies suggest [1]. The central buildings of Machu Picchu are built in classical Inca dry masonry, with large blocks precisely shaped through quarrying, stone-cutting, and stone-dressing, then fitted together without mortar [1]. Machu Picchu was connected to the Inca road system and long-distance trade, as shown by obsidian nodules found near the site’s entrance [1].

row.name: Craterus' ex voto
row.description: The ex voto of Craterus at Delphi was a bronze sculptural group depicting a lion hunt involving Alexander the Great and his general Craterus, attributed to the renowned 4th-century BC sculptors Lysippos and Leochares [1]. French Archaeological School excavations revealed a rectangular building (15.27 x 6.35m) between the Temple of Apollo and the theatre, with walls standing 4m high, likely a portico housing the sculpture on a pedestal against its rear wall [1]. Dedicated posthumously by Craterus' son around 320 BC, the now-lost composition is thought to be echoed in a lion-hunt relief from Messina now in the Louvre [1].

row.name: Rivas District
row.description: A Chiriqui Period (AD 750-1500) archaeological site in the Perez Zeledon canton, San Jose province, Costa Rica, discovered in the 1980s by Robert Drolet [1]. Excavations began in 1992 under Jeffrey Quilter of the Peabody Museum, Harvard University [1]. Over six years, researchers identified residential areas with river cobble structures in circular patterns ranging from 10 to 30 metres in diameter with adjoining rectangular patios [1]. Paths, causeways, plazas, and stairways were recorded throughout [1]. Over 600,000 ceramic sherds were recovered, with 60% of rims decorated in the Buenos Aires Polychrome tradition, considered Chiriqui Period 'fiesta ware' [1].

row.name: Merheleva Ridge
row.description: Merheleva Ridge (Ukrainian: Мергелева гряда) is an Eneolithic temple and burial complex in Luhansk Oblast, Ukraine, featuring four large stone kurgans (mounds) near Perevalsk, approximately 30 km west-southwest of Luhansk [1] [2]. The complex was officially announced on September 7, 2006 [1] [3].

row.name: Colha
row.description: Colha is a Maya archaeological site in northern Belize, about 52 km north of Belize City near Orange Walk [1]. One of the earliest Maya settlements, it was occupied from the Early Preceramic period (3400-1900 BC) through the Middle Postclassic period [1]. Population peaks occurred during the Late Preclassic and Late Classic periods [1]. Colha's trade networks may have extended to the Greater Antilles [1].

row.name: Zyndram's Hill
row.description: Zyndram's Hill (Gora Zyndrama) in Maszkowice, southern Poland, is a prehistoric fortified settlement in the Beskid Wyspowy range of the Northern Carpathians [1]. The site was occupied during the Early Bronze Age (1750-1550 BC), the Late Bronze and Early Iron Age (950-400 BC), and the La Tene period (200-50 BC) [1].

row.name: Tumba Madžari
row.description: Tumba Madžari (6000–4300 BC) is the most significant Neolithic settlement in the Skopje valley, located in north-eastern Skopje, North Macedonia [1]. Discovered in 1961/62 during archaeological trial excavations for motorway construction, the site was first excavated in 1978 by the Museum of Macedonia under Voislav Sanev's leadership [1].

row.name: Warham Camp
row.description: Warham Camp is an Iron Age circular hillfort with a diameter of 212 metres located near Warham, south of Wells-next-the-Sea in Norfolk, England [1] [2]. It is a scheduled monument dated to between 800BC and 43AD [1] [2]. The 5.1-hectare (13-acre) site is designated as a biological Site of Special Scientific Interest and lies within the Norfolk Coast Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty [1] [3]. The University of East Anglia has described it as the best-preserved hill fort in Norfolk [1] [4].

row.old_value: A cave complex from 4300-3500 BC that yielded the world's oldest known leather shoe and the oldest known winery. Both were preserved by dry cave conditions.
row.new_value: In January 2011, the earliest known winery in the world was uncovered in the cave.

row.old_value: A sizeable Maya city from 350 BC buried in dense virgin rainforest, accessible only by mule trail. Its pyramids and causeways remain largely unexcavated.
Latte stone pillars quarried 1.2 km away, from a site occupied as early as 10,000 BC. Only one pillar still stands upright after centuries of earthquakes.
Iron Age defended settlement on Hawkridge Ridge Wood in Somerset, close to Mounsey Castle. Its earthworks survive on a wooded ridge about 3 kilometres from the market town of Dulverton.
The site of ancient Madauros, a Roman colony famed for its schools. The writer Apuleius, author of 'The Golden Ass' — the only surviving complete Roman novel — studied here.
Derventio — the Roman fort at Papcastle — was first built in timber and later rebuilt in stone. The fort's name echoes the Celtic word for oak, preserving a trace of the pre-Roman landscape.
A steep 370 m volcanic hill with an Iron Age fort from around 800 BC. Its fortifications exploited the natural defences of the volcanic terrain.
Oretani tribal capital since at least 600 BC, with Neolithic layers beneath. A local princess named Himilce married Hannibal, sealing the city's alliance in the Second Punic War.
Bronze Age flint tools give way to Cranmore Castle hillfort on Exeter Hill, with a Roman marching camp later sited on the hillside below Knightshayes Court.
Cave with Paleolithic pigment markings -- revealed in a 2021 paper. Art within its chambers pushes the story of early human creativity further back than previously documented in the region.
Pre-Columbian cave with rock art, 22 metres deep and 30 metres wide. Bone remains confirm it served as a burial ground for Inca-era communities in the Cusco highlands.
The first Greek colony on the western mainland, founded by Euboean settlers in the 8th century BC. Its oracle rivaled Delphi, and its alphabet became the basis for Latin script.
A cave occupied from 38,000 BC to 3000 BC — 35,000 years of nearly continuous human use. Obsidian from the island of Melos shows its residents were making sea voyages by 11,000 BC.
Prehistoric archaeological site near Sartène in Corsica — a commune noted for its exceptional concentration of ancient monuments across the southern part of the island.
A settlement at 4,115 metres with the earliest evidence of reduced mobility in the Lake Titicaca Basin, from 3400-1600 BC. Three pithouses were excavated.
Inca hilltop mound overlooking the Cusco valley. Name means 'lake-terrace' in Quechua. Terraced slopes and stone foundations survive, largely unexcavated — one of Cusco's least-visited Inca sites.
4th-3rd millennium BC settlement in Nakhchivan, a 0.8-hectare mound near the Araz River. Ɗrəbyengicə sits at a crossroads of ancient routes linking the South Caucasus to Mesopotamia.
Founded in 396 BC, ancient Tyndaris sits on a dramatic hilltop. Its theatre, basilica, and floor mosaics are still being excavated today.
Rock painting site at 3,782 metres above sea level on the flank of Mount Qayakuna in Pasco Region. The paintings are sheltered at the edge of the high-altitude village of Quchaq.
A site with the highest percentage of horse bones of any contemporary settlement, 4500–3500 BC. A horse burial with bit wear suggests early horse domestication.
The only four-faced triumphal arch still standing in Rome, built in the 4th century AD. Its four passages allowed traffic to flow in every direction through the intersection.
Hilltop settlement northwest of Pallanchacra at 3,167 metres in Pasco Region. Its high-altitude position and commanding views suggest a role in controlling the surrounding Andean valleys.
A village on the ancient Icknield Way, claimed to be Britain's oldest road. The Upper and Lower Icknield routes converge here, though the claim is debated.
4th–1st millennium BC. Moylehid in Fermanagh contains the Eagle's Knoll Cairn Passage Tomb — a scheduled monument in a townland occupied for thousands of years; its name means 'hill of breadth'.
A 1900–1650 BC village with multi-room rectangular houses — early examples of that domestic form in the region. Cattle, deer, pig, and goat bones document what its inhabitants ate.
A walled Roman city from the 1st century AD that grew into one of Moesia's largest urban centers. Emperor Decius was killed fighting Goths near here in 251 AD.

3rd-millennium BC village at 820 m in the Kakheti highlands, investigated since the 1960s. Stone artefacts at Ziari testify to Palaeolithic workshops - a site far older than its Bronze Age occupation.
A 1974 sanctuary protecting the battlefield of Junin and ruins of the Pumpush culture. Before the Incas, the Pumpush and Yarovilca peoples farmed this plateau.
Built in the late 4th or early 3rd millennium BC near the Dolmen de Menga, this passage tomb was constructed by the same community that raised its larger neighbour just 70 metres away.
A Bronze Age landscape on Dartmoor with stone rows, a stone circle, standing stones, and burial cairns. The sheer density of monuments suggests this moorland held deep ritual significance.
Inca site on top of Allqu Willka mountain in the Huanta highlands, active 1438–1530 AD. High-altitude summit sites in the Inca world typically combined administrative, military, and ritual functions.
Inca-period archaeological site north of San Jeronimo in the Cusco Region, part of the pre-Columbian settlement network spread across the highland terrain.
Hundreds of round stone structures spread across 207 square kilometres of Andean cloud forest, claimed as a pre-Columbian Chachapoyas city. The identification remains disputed among historians.

Roughly triangular with an area still undefined, this Somerset promontory fort sits above Clatworthy Reservoir. Its history spans the Bronze to Iron Ages, and it sits on the Heritage at Risk Register.
A 1700 BC Minoan temple destroyed by earthquake during what appears to be a human sacrifice in progress. A skeleton with a bronze blade lay on the altar.
Inca site with two platforms — Hatun and Huch'uy Quri Wayrachina — near Mount Inka Pallanka, still venerated as an apu by locals. Active 1438–1530 AD in the Lucanas Province of Ayacucho.
Necropolis near Pydna, spanning Bronze Age to early Christian times. Tomb finds reveal a shrinking population during the second colonisation wave -- the dead recording a slow civilisational decline.
Ruins identified as two ancient cities destroyed by Philip II of Macedon around 346 BC. Neither was ever rebuilt — both simply ceased to exist.
1st-century AD Roman settlement in Pannonia, sited on the road between Poetovio and Siscia. Believed to lie near today's village of Komin — a minor node in Rome's Danubian road network.
Two Macedonian tombs at the site of ancient Pydna, where Alexander the Great's dynasty ended in 168 BC. Tomb A, the larger one, was found intact with its grave goods undisturbed.
Active 800 BC-900 AD, K'axob began as a Late Preclassic Maya village on two pyramid plazas and grew through the Classic Period. It lies in the Pulltrouser Swamp wetlands of northern Mesoamerica.
Inca site atop Jatunhosno mountain in the Ayacucho highlands, active 1438–1530 AD. High-altitude summit sites in the Inca world typically combined administrative, military, and ritual functions.
Over 40 barrows clustered at Upper Lambourn, Berkshire, the earliest dating to c. 2200 BC. The 4-hectare site is also a biological SSSI — its chalk grassland supports more than 100 herb species.
Twin deep ditches and ramparts crown this Wiltshire hilltop on the ancient Ridgeway. In 556 AD Saxons fought a decisive battle here that helped forge the future kingdom of Wessex.
Active 400 BC-900 AD, Ka'Kabish held 90 structures across 8 groups: two major temples, a ballcourt with circular marker, and large platforms that likely served as royal or elite residences.
1st century AD Roman theatre ruins in the city of Rome — one of the entertainment venues of the imperial capital, now standing in partial ruin among the monuments of the ancient city.
A Neolithic settlement from the 5th millennium BC where pottery and stone tools were found. The earliest layers of habitation in this region date to this period.
Hilltop fort on a Devon ridgeline above valleys formed by Coly River tributaries. The terrain provided natural defence on three sides, concentrating fortification on the exposed eastern approach.
T-shaped stone monuments up to 5 m tall, found only on Menorca. Built 500–300 BC, their exact purpose—religious, astronomical, or both—remains unknown.
A Chimu adobe palace from around 900 AD with three terraces covered in zoomorphic and geometric friezes. Linked to the capital Chan Chan during the empire's rise.
A Paleolithic settlement known for engraved mammoth-ivory bracelets with geometric patterns. Some researchers argue the marks are the earliest known attempt at musical notation.
1st-century AD Roman city on the Via Militaris between Naissus and Serdica. Its bishop Nicetas (c.335–414), patron saint of Romania, is credited by many scholars as author of the Te Deum.
A Harappan-era settlement occupied from 3000 to 1900 BC, just 6 km from the even older site of Mehrgarh. Together they span 7,000 years of continuous civilization.
Contains 71 hand stencils cataloged using ultraviolet photography. A 2018 study dated one to 66,700 years ago — making it Neanderthal art, not human.
Neolithic tor enclosure at Redruth occupied 3700-3400 BC, with stone walls and an earth bank securing the summit. Evidence of organised violence makes it among the earliest fortified sites known.
An Iron Age fortified camp at Bulstrode Park survives here. The builders chose a strategic position in the Chiltern foothills above the River Misbourne.
Built as a Bronze Age burial chamber on Exmoor, it later marked the corner of four parishes simultaneously. Its name evolved from Osmunesburgh (13th c.) to Owlaman's Burrow before settling in 1782.
A 1st-century AD Roman funerary tower standing along the Via Augusta. Its carved relief figures were long mistaken for the Scipio brothers, giving it its name.
A Bronze Age tell-mound formed by mudbrick settlement collapse and rebuilding - the Aegean equivalent of a Near Eastern tell. Each layer conceals a distinct era of prehistoric northern occupation.
Four uprights bear a tilting capstone at the north-west tip of Islandmagee — known locally as the Druid's Altar, dating to around 2000 BC or the stripped remains of an earlier passage grave.
Perched above Clevedon with steep natural slopes to south and north and two ramparts closing the eastern approach, this univallate fort guards a river valley entrance in North Somerset.
Founded by Messapians in the 8th c. BC, Rudiae covered 100 hectares — twice the size of nearby Lecce. A 2011 dig uncovered an amphitheatre seating 8,000. Birthplace of the poet Ennius.
A Roman road branching off Dere Street, traceable for 89 km north. Like many Roman roads, it got a "Devil" nickname in the Middle Ages.
A 1st-century BC altar where representatives of 60 Gallic tribes gathered annually to pledge loyalty to Rome. It was the political center of Roman-controlled Gaul.
A double-banked Iron Age fort covering 3.4 hectares, dating to around 50 BC. Its multivallate design suggests a community expecting serious threats.
400 BC-1000 AD Maya site partly buried under a modern town. Main Palace blends Chenes decorated facades with Rio Bec design; ceramics push its origins back to the Middle Preclassic period.
A city-kingdom from the 13th century BC. Its most famous son, Zeno of Citium (born c. 334 BC), founded Stoicism -- one of antiquity's most influential philosophies.
3rd-4th century AD Roman mausoleum complex spanning 25 hectares. Built during the Tetrarchy in Dacia Ripensis with 32-bastion walls and a crypted basilica - discovered by Dragoslav Srejovic.
A 1st-century AD Roman marching camp at the site of modern Hamburg, built where ships from Flevum could dock. Rome abandoned it when the frontier pulled back to the Rhine.
A Neolithic dolmen measuring 3.25 by 2.95 metres and a tumulus nearby — both listed as historical monuments. The dolmen is known locally as the Dolmen des Bignes.
Settled from 6000 BC, this fortified city produced the world's earliest known alphabet around 1300 BC. Its 90-room royal palace and twin temples crowned a 20-meter mound.
Roman defensive walls built around Durnovaria starting about 130 AD. The earthen bank and stone walls were recut in the medieval period and became public walks.
A village 50 km northwest of Niš, recorded in Roman times as Cametas. The name means "stake" locally, and the municipality retains visible remnants of its Roman-era past.
Minoan through Roman ruins blanket this uninhabited islet 5.6 km off eastern Crete. Known in antiquity as Leuce, Koufonisi bears centuries of occupation visible above and below the Libyan Sea.
4th-century BC monument at Delphi built by Craterus, Alexander's general, attributed to Lysippos. A 15 x 6.35 m building between the Temple of Apollo and the theatre.
A settlement occupied 750–1500 AD near a major tectonic boundary. The Talamancan people built communities on geologically volatile land.
An Eneolithic temple and burial complex of four large stone kurgans. The site preserves rituals from the Copper Age, when the first metal tools were changing human society.
One of the earliest Maya sites, occupied 3400 BC-1300 AD — spanning the full arc of Maya civilisation. A specialist tool-production centre supplying tools across the northern Maya lowlands.
A prehistoric hilltop settlement occupied in the Early Bronze Age, Late Bronze Age, and La Tene period. Its defensive position 410 meters up controlled a Carpathian pass.
Neolithic settlement occupied 6000-4300 BC near modern Skopje - the most significant in the valley. Found during motorway construction in 1961, its stratigraphy maps layers of early farming life.
A 4000 BC dolmen whose capstone bears a carved axe and a plough pulled by oxen. The capstone was part of a broken menhir—the carving matches across the break.
A perfectly circular Iron Age fort with a 212-meter diameter, dating to around 300 BC. A later river channel was cut straight through the middle, splitting it in two.
A stone Roman theatre built in 161 AD with a three-story facade and a wooden roof of Lebanese cedar. It seated 5,000 and still hosts concerts on the slopes of the Acropolis.
row.new_value: The Odeon of Herodes Atticus is a stone Greek theatre structure located on the southwest slope of the Acropolis of Athens.

row.old_value: A 15th-century Inca citadel at 2,430 metres, built from polished dry-stone walls without mortar. Its Intihuatana stone was precisely carved to track the sun through the solstices.
row.new_value: Studies of skeletal remains found at Machu Picchu show that most people who lived there were immigrants from diverse backgrounds.

row.old_value: In January 2011, the earliest known winery in the world was uncovered in the cave.
A Roman port at the closest point to continental Europe. It grew into the gateway between Britain and Gaul — an essential cross-channel hub.
Part of the Cotzumalhuapa zone, occupied from around 1000 BC. A stela here bears a Long Count date from the late pre-Classic era — one of the earliest such dates outside the core Maya lowlands.
A walled Chachapoya city from the 6th century AD with 421 circular stone buildings. Some walls stand 2 metres high with carved friezes of faces and patterns.
A Roman fort built on a mountain pass between 120 and 138 AD, garrisoned by troops from the Dalmatian coast. A parade ground leveled into the steep hillside still survives.

row.old_value: About 30 pre-Inca chullpa burial towers perched at 3,000 metres elevation. Chullpas were built so the dead could face the rising sun in an eternal vigil.
The Odeon of Herodes Atticus is a stone Greek theatre structure located on the southwest slope of the Acropolis of Athens.
Ruins of a large Jewish village from the Roman-Byzantine period, with an ancient synagogue and mausoleum. It may be the lost town of Teqoa of Galilee.
A fortress city guarding the only two mountain passes into Thessaly from the north. Whoever held Gonnus controlled access to the Thessalian plain.
Built in stone around 124 AD, this auxiliary fort on Hadrian's Wall housed up to 800 infantry. Its communal latrines — stone benches over a flushing sewer — survive in remarkable condition.

row.old_value: A Roman temple to Augustus built 27 BC–14 AD with a richly decorated frieze. It survived by being repurposed as a church, then a granary, then a museum.
Studies of skeletal remains found at Machu Picchu show that most people who lived there were immigrants from diverse backgrounds.
About 337 meters long and 160 meters wide, this Herefordshire fort overlooks the confluence of the Wye and Lugg rivers from a spur of Dinedor Hill. Its out-turned east entrance is still visible.
A Roman villa built in phases from the 2nd to 5th century, among the largest in Roman Britain. Its elaborate 4th-century mosaics survive in vivid detail.
Founded 480 BC on the Gulf of Saint Euphemia, Terina minted silver coins celebrated across the Mediterranean for their artistry. Hannibal razed the city during the Second Punic War.
Limestone caves with evidence of habitation from 11,000 BC to the 3rd century AD. The larger cave has nine chambers connected by narrow passages, with sinkholes letting in daylight.
A 4th-century BC healing center combining medicine, religion, and psychology. Treatments included dream interpretation, mud baths, and herbal remedies.

Excavated ground at the foot of Mount Meron exceeded six acres. Khirbet Shema holds a large Jewish village of the Roman and Byzantine periods, with its synagogue and mausoleum.
At Church Stoke in eastern Montgomeryshire, a steep-sided volcanic hill rises to 370 metres. Roundton Hill has been a nature reserve of the Montgomeryshire Wildlife Trust since 1985.
Gonnus stood on the north side of the Peneius, near the entrance of the only two passes by which an enemy could enter Thessaly from the north. Xerxes I's army came that way.
A causeway links El Tintal to El Mirador, the larger site. About 25 km northeast of Carmelita, El Tintal is the second-largest in the Mirador Basin, among the four largest in northern Petén.
Near Linares, Castulo was occupied from the Neolithic period and by the 6th century BC was the chief settlement of the Oretani. Roman sources say the princess Himilce married Hannibal.
Where the Exe and Lowman meet, Stone Age flint tools mark Tiverton, the town on two fords. Cranmore Castle, over 15 acres, possibly a livestock enclosure, market site or tribal oppidum.
An earthquake in 1821 revealed the Cave of Ardales in Malaga province, where over 1,000 paintings and engravings lie across the walls, the ceilings and the speleothems.
In Chinchaypujio District of Cusco, Pumawasi is a pre-Columbian rock art cave 22 m deep, 30 m wide and 19 m high. Ceramics and human bone remains show burial ground and ceremonial use.
Cumae, the first Greek colony on mainland Italy, was founded around 725 BC from Chalcis. Famed as the home of the Cumaean Sibyl, it holds a purported 130-metre underground corridor.
Franchthi Cave overlooks Kiladha Bay, where finds trace the transition from Paleolithic hunter-gatherers to Neolithic farmers, with domesticated plants and animals appearing around 7,000 BC.
Near Sartène in the Sartenais region of southern Corsica, Apazzu is a prehistoric megalithic site. Excavations uncovered artifacts, among them a stone vase with a zoomorphic protome.
54 km southeast of Puno in the Titicaca Basin, Jisk'a Iru Muqu was occupied from circa 3400-1600 BCE. Excavations recovered obsidian tools, a gold necklace and early domestic architecture.
In the district of Huayopata, La Convención Province, in the Cusco region of Peru, an archaeological site carries two spellings: Cochapata, also written Qochapata.
Dubris, on the site of Dover, became the main Roman cross-Channel port, taking over from Rutupiae. A 1970s bypass uncovered its remains; an eight-week excavation found a Roman mansio.
M'Daourouch sits at the site of the ancient Berber-Roman town of Madauros in Numidia. Two names, one piece of ground: Madauros for the ancient town, M'Daourouch for the site standing there.
On a spur of Dinedor Hill, Dinedor Camp looks east to where the Wye meets the Lugg. In 1951 a trench was cut from the rampart edge about 35 metres towards the centre of the camp.
About 200 meters north of the Araz River, Ərəbyengicə is an ancient settlement whose finds include obsidian remains and combed-surface pottery of the Late Chalcolithic.
Tindari's Greek theater, built between the 4th and 3rd centuries BC, could seat 3,000 spectators. In the 1st century AD part of the cliff collapsed; earthquakes did more in the 4th century.
Near the village of Ninamaca, about 30 chullpas of pre-Inca times stand on top of a mountain at about 3,000 m. Ninamarca is possibly Quechua nina, fire, and marka, village: fire village.
Digging for a ferret in 1864, a gamekeeper uncovered Chedworth Roman Villa, one of the largest Roman villas found in Britain. Its west wing held a mosaic dining-room and two bathing suites.
At Hartashen Megalithic Avenue, two avenues of basalt menhirs stand at an angle in three rows each, and the lines never meet. What the rows were for is unclear; the site has no firm dating.
At the foot of the mountain Qayakuna, in the village of Quchaq north of the town Cerro de Pasco, Qaqapatan keeps its rock paintings high at approximately 3,782 metres.
Deriivka, a Copper Age site on the Dnieper, gave up a horse burial with apparent bit wear, first read as the earliest evidence of riding. Radiocarbon dating put the skull in the Iron Age.
Four faces, four passages: the Arch of Janus is the only surviving quadrifrons arch in Rome, 16 m high in the Forum Boarium. Built from older spolia, it may honor Constantine I.
Guellayhuasin is an archaeological site in Peru's Pasco region, at an elevation of 3,167 m, northwest of the village of Pallanchacra. High Pasco ground, and a site marked out on it.
Inside the Chiltern Hills, Ivinghoe keeps an Anglo-Saxon name glossed as 'Ifa's hill-spur'. In 1086 the Domesday Book wrote it Evinghehou, and St Mary was burnt in 1234, rebuilt in 1241.
Two monuments stand in the townland of Moylehid, County Fermanagh: the Eagle's Knoll Cairn passage tomb and the Moylehid ring cairn, named from the Irish Mul-leithid, hill of breadth.
Cattle, deer, pig and goat bones lay beside the ceramics at Alampra, a Middle Bronze Age settlement of circa 1900-1650 BC in Cyprus, dug by John E. Coleman between 1974 and 1985.
Founded as a military camp near modern Razgrad, Abritus was a major Roman fortified city. Excavations there brought up Bulgaria's largest Late Antique gold treasure: 835 coins weighing 4 kg.
In the Kakheti region of Georgia, research at Ziari in Gurjaani Municipality has, since the 1960s, unearthed numerous stone artifacts, testifying to the presence of Paleolithic workshops.
Brewer's Castle: a pear-shaped Iron Age enclosure just under 0.4 ha, the River Barle on three sides and Dane's Brook to the south-west, on a steep, flat-topped knoll.
Chacamarca Historic Sanctuary: 2,500 hectares at approximately 4,105 metres, where patriot forces under Bolivar routed royalist troops on 6 August 1824, protecting Pumpush remains.
Papcastle was Derventio, a Roman fort built in timber and later rebuilt in stone. Excavations from 2010-2015 found one of the most complete Roman water mills in Britain.
By the EX-214 road, the Dolmen del prado de Lácara was built toward the end of the 4th millennium BC, or in the early 3rd millennium BC, among Extremadura's most monumental megalithic sites.
On western Dartmoor, Merrivale holds double stone rows, the longest 263 metres, a circle of 11 granite stones about 18 metres across, and a standing menhir over 3 metres tall.
On top of the mountain Allqu Willka in Ayacucho, Inka Raqay is an Inca site, and raqay in Quechua means a ruin, a shed, a storehouse, or a dormitory for farm laborers.
Cheqollo means nightingale in Quechua. Its pre-Hispanic site lies north of San Jeronimo in Peru's Cusco Region, within a landscape of deep Inca and pre-Inca heritage.
Gran Saposoa: ruins in the Andean cloud forests, brought to attention by Gene Savoy in 1999. Scholars dispute his claims: Muscutt and Schjellerup had located them in the mid-1990s.
An Iron Age hill fort 3 miles north west of Wiveliscombe: Clatworthy Camp is an Ancient Monument on the Heritage at Risk Register, vulnerable to scrub and tree growth.
Destroyed by earthquake around 1700 BC, the Minoan temple of Anemospilia on Mount Juktas held a young man on an altar with a bronze blade, read as sacrifice, still debated.
Quriwayrachina, an Inca-period site in Peru's Ayacucho Region, keeps two platforms, Hatun Quri Wayrachina and Huch'uy Quri Wayrachina, near the mountain Inka Pallanka, venerated as an apu.
Along the old road from Methone to Dion, the Necropolises of Pydna hold Macedonian tombs from the Bronze Age to the early Christian period; smaller tumuli are lost to erosion.
Desfina is a town in southern Phocis. On the hill of Kastrouli nearby, a fortified Mycenaean settlement of the 13th-12th century BC has been tentatively identified with Homeric Anemoreia.
Near the Areni village along the Arpa River, Areni-1 Cave gave up the earliest known shoe in the world, the oldest humanoid brain, and a straw skirt dating to 3,900 years BCE.
A Roman road ran from Poetovio in the north to Siscia in the south, and Pyrri stood along it in Pannonia. Evidence suggests the settlement lies under the village of Komin today.
Near the modern village of Korinos, on the site of ancient Pydna, the Macedonian Tombs hold Tomb A, discovered in the mid-19th century, and a second smaller grave, Tomb B, found in 1991.
Kʼaxob was a Maya site in Belize, occupied from about 800 BC to AD 900. It began as a village and grew through the Early to Late Classic Periods into household mounds and plazas.
In the Ayacucho Region of Peru, Hatun Usnu means big usnu in Quechua: a pyramid-shaped, terraced ceremonial platform the Incas used for rituals involving liquid offerings.
Seven Barrows is a Bronze Age barrow cemetery at Upper Lambourn in Berkshire, England. Its unimproved chalk grassland supports over 100 herb species and a rich insect fauna.
On Barbury Hill in Wiltshire, about 5.5 miles south of Swindon, the Iron Age hillfort of Barbury Castle keeps two deep defensive ditches and ramparts beside the ancient Ridgeway route.
At the end of the 1-mile-long crag of the Whin Sill, Hadrian's Wall runs over the fort at Housesteads, whose stone walls were built around AD 124 above a demolished turret.
KaʼKabish lies in Belize's Orange Walk District, near Lamanai, El Pozito and Blue Creek. Three neighbouring places, and the district in Belize that holds the site.
In Aosta in Italy, the Teatro Romano was built during the Julio-Claudian dynasty. Its 22-metre-high facade wall still towers over the city, and the theatre hosts performances today.
Near Porodin, near Bitola, the Neolithic settlement of Veluška Tumba is a raised mound shaped like a truncated cone, 250 m long and 150 m wide, holding a cultural layer four metres thick.
Near Southleigh in Devon, the Iron Age hillfort of Blackbury Camp encloses roughly 200 m by 100 m behind a rampart about 3 m high, and excavations uncovered over 1,000 slingstones.
On Menorca, Taula is a megalithic structure: a vertical pillar supporting a horizontal capstone, reaching heights of up to 5 metres. Its exact purpose remains unknown.
A local landowner uncovered Huaca Esmeralda from the sand in 1923; the Chimu pyramid in Trujillo shows relief of fishing nets and fish on two platforms of approximately 65 by 41 meters.
On the southwest slope of the Acropolis of Athens, the stone Odeon of Herodes Atticus was completed in AD 161. Its stands and orchestra were restored in Pentelic marble in the 1950s.
On the Desna River bank, Mezine holds Ukraine's most Paleolithic artifact finds: bracelets engraved with marks possibly marking lunar cycles, and the earliest known meander pattern.
On the Piano di Tirena hill in Calabria, Terina lies between the Savuto and the Grande and matches a description Strabo wrote around 20 AD. Its coins and inscriptions rest in Lamezia Terme.
Remesiana lay beneath modern Bela Palanka on the Via Militaris, a major early Christian center under Bishop Nicetas. In 1987 it was declared an Archaeological Site of Great Importance.
At Nausharo, 6 km from Mehrgarh, a pottery workshop gave up fired and unfired pottery, unworked clay and 12 flint blades or blade fragments, plus copper traces on two blade platforms.
In 1951 a quarry explosion exposed the Cave of Maltravieso in Caceres. Inside, 71 hands were stencilled onto the walls, together with linear designs and animal paintings.
Carn Brea, 1.6 km southwest of Redruth, crowns a hilltop in Cornwall, a fortified Neolithic settlement occupied between 3700 and 3400 BC, ringed by a 4.5-hectare outer rampart.
Three sinkholes drop natural light into the nine chambers of the larger Padah-Lin cave. In the smaller rock shelter, red ochre hands, fish, bulls and bison mark the rock.
Gerrards Cross lies on the lower slopes of the Chiltern Hills near the River Misbourne, and the area around it holds Bulstrode Park Camp, an Iron Age fortified encampment.
El Baúl, part of the Cotzumalhuapa Archaeological Zone, was occupied during the Formative stage; its southern acropolis was destroyed in 1997 and its main groups now lie under sugar cane.
Kuélap stands on a limestone ridge at 3000 metres, its walls 10 to 20 m high and all but five of its 421 structures circular. It was rediscovered in 1843 by Juan Crisóstomo Nieto.
On Exmoor, the turf-covered Bronze Age bowl barrow Alderman's Barrow measures 24 by 22 meters and stands 1.4 meters high. In the 13th century it was called Osmunesburgh.
Along the Via Augusta, 6 km from ancient Tarraco, Torre dels Escipions rises, a Roman funerary tower of the early 1st century AD, likely a family mausoleum holding cremated remains.
In northern Greece, Toumba is the Greek name for the mounds Bronze Age settlements left behind. What the settlements left in the ground, and the word the mounds carry.
In a private front garden on the Islandmagee peninsula stands Ballylumford Dolmen, known locally as the Druid's Altar: four upright stones under a heavy capstone, and a fallen stone inside.
Approximately 1.6 km south-west of Clevedon in North Somerset, Wain's Hill is an Iron Age bivallate hillfort: linear earthwork banks and ditches on steep slopes.
Strabo called Rudiae a Greek city. In the immediate outskirts of Lecce, its remains still show traces of an amphitheatre, a necropolis and two city walls built of tuff.
The Devil's Causeway is a Roman road in Northumberland: it branches off Dere Street north of Corbridge and runs approximately 55 miles north to Berwick-upon-Tweed.
The Asclepieion of Pergamon was a healing temple for Asclepius and Hygieia, founded in the mid-4th century BCE as a modest spring shrine and built up over roughly eight centuries.
Drusus founded the Ara trium Galliarum at Lugdunum, where the Rhone and Saone meet, as a sanctuary to Roma and Augustus. Its altar bore the names of 60 Gallic tribes.
The House of Taga on Tinian held twelve prehistoric megaliths standing approximately 15 feet tall, each a base crowned by a hemispherical capstone. Only one still stands.
Dating to approximately 50 BC, Ringsbury Camp is an Iron Age multivallate hillfort whose double banks were built from non-local limestone rubble. Its inner bank rises 5 metres high.
Occupied from around 500 BC, Dzibilnocac grew into a Maya city whose Chenes facades are elaborately decorated, while the main Palace carries a distinct Rio Bec design.
The Peterborough Petroglyphs, cut in the pre-Columbian era, are the largest collection of First Nations rock carvings in Ontario: shamans, animals, reptiles, possibly the Great Spirit.
Phoenicians from Tyre revived Kition in the 9th century BC. Its Bamboula acropolis still shows ship sheds for triremes and a sanctuary dating to at least the 9th century BC.
Vrelo Šarkamen spans 25 hectares on the slopes of Deli Jovan in eastern Serbia, a Roman residential and memorial complex with a mausoleum. Only ruins remain today.
Treva is the historical name of a Roman-era settlement in Germany, first recorded by Claudius Ptolemy in the 2nd century AD. Under Augustus, Roman forces reached the Elbe.

In the Orne department of Normandy, Habloville holds two Neolithic monuments: a stone table measuring 3.25 by 2.95 metres, and just to the south a listed tumulus.
The Temple of Augustus, probably built between 27 BC and AD 14, measures about 8 by 17.3 m and 14 m high, its tetrastyle prostyle porch of Corinthian columns standing on a podium.
At Ras Shamra the port city of Ugarit held a royal palace of many courtyards and two acropolis temples to Baal and Dagan; its excavated texts echo Hebrew biblical poetry.
The Town Walks of Dorchester follow the line of the Roman defences of Durnovaria, its ruined walls landscaped into tree-lined avenues between 1702 and 1743. Only one wall fragment survives.
Ražanj stands on the ancient Via Militaris, the Roman military highway. The settlement on it was known as Cametas in Roman times, and finds from building work confirm prehistoric habitation.
Koufonisi is an uninhabited islet in the Libyan Sea, 5.6 km south of cape Goudero on Crete's eastern coast. Through the summer, tour boats cross from the port of Makry Gialos.
Hardknott Roman Fort, the remains of Mediobogdum, stands on the western side of the challenging Hardknott Pass. Leather objects from its Roman occupation have been found here.
At 2,430 meters, about 104 caves and rock shelters around Machu Picchu held the remains of about 174 individuals, interpreted largely as yanaconas rather than the Inca elite.
Craterus' ex voto at Delphi was a bronze lion hunt with Alexander the Great. French excavations uncovered walls standing 4m high between the Temple of Apollo and the theatre.
Rivas District, a Chiriqui Period site of AD 750-1500, gave up residential areas of river cobbles laid in circles 10 to 30 metres across. Paths, plazas and stairways were recorded here.
In Luhansk Oblast, Ukraine, the Merheleva Ridge is an Eneolithic temple and burial complex of four large stone kurgans, officially announced on September 7, 2006.
Colha, one of the earliest Maya settlements, was occupied from 3400-1900 BC in the Early Preceramic period through the Middle Postclassic. Its trade may have reached the Greater Antilles.
Zyndram's Hill, a prehistoric fortified settlement in the Beskid Wyspowy range, was occupied in the Early Bronze Age, 1750-1550 BC, and in the La Tene period, 200-50 BC.
Tumba Madžari, a Neolithic settlement in the Skopje valley, was uncovered in 1961/62 during trial excavations for a motorway. The Museum of Macedonia first excavated it in 1978.
Table des Marchand is a dolmen on the megalithic site of Locmariaquer in Morbihan, Brittany, standing with the grand broken menhir of Er Grah and the tumulus of Er Grah.
South of Wells-next-the-Sea in Norfolk, Warham Camp is an Iron Age circular hillfort 212 metres in diameter, a scheduled monument dated to between 800BC and 43AD.
